Sorting algorithms. A sorting algorithm is a procedure that arranges elements of a list into a specified order—usually ascending or descending. Sorting is one of the most fundamental and well-studied problems in computer science. Dozens of algorithms exist, and they trade off time complexity, space complexity, stability—which means preserving the relative order of equal elements—and cache behavior. Efficient sorting is essential for search, particularly for binary search which requires a sorted input, for data analysis, and for countless applications. The best comparison-based sorting algorithms achieve O of n log n time, while non-comparative sorting like counting sort and radix sort can achieve linear O of n time under restrictive assumptions about the data.

Let's start with the classic comparison-based sorts. Merge sort uses a divide-and-conquer strategy. It runs in O of n log n time, uses O of n extra space, and is stable. The algorithm splits the list in half recursively and merges the sorted halves back together. Quicksort is also divide-and-conquer. Its average case is O of n log n, but the worst case is O of n squared. It uses O of log n space for the recursion stack and is usually in-place. Quicksort partitions the list via a pivot element, but it's prone to worst-case behavior on already-sorted input unless the pivot selection is randomized. Heap sort uses a heap data structure, runs in guaranteed O of n log n time, uses only O of one constant space, but it's not stable. The algorithm builds a max-heap and repeatedly extracts the maximum. Insertion sort runs in O of n squared time, uses O of one space, is stable, and works in-place. It's efficient on small arrays and nearly-sorted data, so it's often used as a sub-algorithm in hybrid sorts like Timsort. Bubble sort runs in O of n squared time, uses O of one space, is stable, and works in-place, but it's rarely used in practice because of its poor performance.

Then there are the non-comparative sorts. Counting sort runs in O of n plus k time, where k is the range of input values. It requires integer inputs in a small range and is stable. Radix sort runs in O of n times d time, where d is the number of digits. It sorts by each digit position from least significant to most significant and is stable. It's particularly useful for strings and large integers. Bucket sort averages O of n plus k time by distributing elements into buckets, sorting each bucket, and concatenating the results.

Several key concepts unify sorting algorithm design. Stability means that equal elements retain their original relative order. This is important for multi-key sorting—when you need to sort by name and then by age while keeping the age ordering stable. In-place means the algorithm uses only O of one extra space besides the input. Merge sort requires O of n space, while quicksort is typically in-place. Adaptive sorts improve their running time on nearly-sorted input. Insertion sort is highly adaptive, and Timsort explicitly exploits runs of already-sorted elements. There's also a fundamental lower bound for comparison sorting: any comparison-based sort requires at least Omega of n log n comparisons in the worst case. This comes from an information-theoretic argument: there are n factorial possible orderings of n elements, and you need log base two of n factorial, which is approximately n log n bits, to distinguish them.

Modern systems use adaptive, hybrid algorithms tuned for real-world distributions and cache behavior. Timsort is a hybrid of merge sort and insertion sort used in Python and Java. It has O of n log n worst-case time but O of n best-case time on nearly-sorted data, and it's stable. Introsort is a hybrid of quicksort and heap sort. It starts with quicksort and switches to heap sort if recursion depth exceeds two log n. This is used in C++ standard library sort. In practice, most systems don't use pure sorting algorithms anymore; they use these adaptive variants.

Sorting is a canonical problem in computer science. It teaches fundamental algorithmic thinking, Big O analysis, and divide-and-conquer strategy. The problem is so well-studied that it serves as a benchmark for new algorithmic techniques and hardware. The earliest electronic computers like ENIAC were measured partly on their sorting throughput. The transition from O of n squared algorithms to O of n log n optimal algorithms illustrates how algorithmic insight can provide exponential speedup as data sizes grow. Sorting has deep connections to other domains: sorting networks, which are specialized circuits for parallel sorting; external sorting for data larger than RAM; parallel sorting algorithms; and specialized sorts for strings and integers all require distinct insights. In job interviews and algorithm competitions, sorting is ubiquitous. It's not just "implement quicksort," but rather "solve this problem efficiently using sorting" or "derive a sorting algorithm adapted to this specific constraint." Understanding the tradeoffs between sorts is essential for choosing the right tool in practice.
